_comment: Source of the certification assessment. 'answer' is the id of the correct option. The build script replaces it with a salted hash before anything is shipped to browsers. Keep this file out of any published artifact.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of Daily Work Management (DWM)?

options.t: To run routine work to standard every day, check results against targets and act on abnormalities, so performance is maintained and improved.
To produce daily reports for senior management.
To replace improvement projects with daily meetings.
To record operator mistakes for appraisal.

questions.explain: DWM turns objectives and standards into routine execution, monitoring and corrective action.

questions.text: The plant objective is to improve on-time delivery. A curing supervisor asks how this affects their shift. What is the best answer?

options.t: It doesn't; delivery is a dispatch department matter.
Through the MP/CP Tree the objective breaks down into measures such as shift output and press uptime, with targets on the MP Planning Sheet that the shift tracks and acts on.
The supervisor should work overtime whenever delivery is late.
Only the plant head needs to know the objective.

questions.explain: Organisational objectives flow down into measures each role can control and review daily.

questions.text: Which document defines a role's responsibilities, including the measures it must manage and review?

options.t: Role Sheet
Shift attendance register
Customer complaint log
Purchase order

questions.explain: The Role Sheet links the organisation structure to each role's duties and measures; standards define how the work is done.

questions.text: What is the difference between the MP/CP Tree and the MP Planning Sheet?

options.t: They are two names for the same document.
The Tree lists employees; the Planning Sheet lists machines.
The Tree shows how result measures (MPs) break down into the process measures (CPs) that drive them; the Planning Sheet sets each measure's target, frequency, method, data source, owner and response.
The Planning Sheet is only used for annual budgets.

questions.explain: The Tree shows cause-and-effect logic; the Planning Sheet turns it into a routine.

questions.text: A new line is being set up. The manager proposes copying another line's output target 'because the lines look similar'. What should you advise?

options.t: Accept it; consistency across lines matters most.
Set it 20% higher to create a stretch.
Let the first week's actual output become the target.
Derive the target from customer demand and the approved plan, and check it against this line's process capability and constraints.

questions.explain: Targets must be aligned with demand and plans and be realistic for the specific process, not copied or arbitrary.

questions.text: Which measure most needs continuous or near-real-time monitoring with an alarm?

options.t: Monthly training hours
Curing platen temperature and pressure, which affect cure quality and safety
Office stationery stock
Weekly canteen feedback score

questions.explain: Frequency follows risk, speed of change, response time, customer and safety impact, and the control plan.

questions.text: Plan is 1,000 tyres per 8-hour shift (125/h). At the 6-hour checkpoint the actual is 570. What is the correct reading?

options.t: On track, because 2 hours remain.
Ahead of plan.
180 tyres behind the expected 750, so verify and act within the shift.
No conclusion is possible until the shift ends.

questions.explain: Compare the actual with the expected-to-date figure at each checkpoint to act early.

questions.text: At the DWM station a team member suggests lowering today's target because the line is behind. What should the reviewer say?

options.t: No. The target stays as approved; we record the gap, find out why and act. Targets change only through the approved planning process.
Yes, it keeps morale high.
Yes, but only on the board, not in the system.
Remove the target from the board for today.

questions.explain: Changing a target to make actual performance look acceptable hides problems.

questions.text: Which is the best abnormality record entry?

options.t: Press problem again, operator careless.
Line 2 CP-04, Shift A 06:52–11:40: 5 stops, alarm 'platen steam pressure low', 46 min lost, 48 tyres on hold. Evidence: PLC log, hold tag QH-0412.
Many stops today.
Boiler issue suspected; no action needed.

questions.explain: Record what, where, when and how big, with evidence, and no blame or unverified cause.

questions.text: Green tyres from one building drum are found underweight at the 18:00 check; 17:00 was in spec. What is the right containment?

options.t: Send them on; final inspection will catch defects.
Hold only the two tyres that were checked.
Segregate and tag all tyres from that drum since the last good check, and inform Quality per the hold procedure.
Scrap the entire day's production immediately.

questions.explain: Containment covers all potentially affected product back to the last good check; release is by Quality.

questions.text: In a Why-Why Analysis, when should the team stop asking 'why'?

options.t: After exactly five whys.
When someone to blame has been identified.
After the first answer, to save time.
When an evidence-supported, controllable cause is reached that explains all the facts, and it can be verified.

questions.explain: There is no fixed number of whys; each step needs evidence, and blame is not a root cause.

questions.text: A press stops repeatedly; each reset restores production but the stops return. Which is a corrective action?

options.t: Reset the press faster each time.
Revise the PM standard to include the inspection whose absence caused the strainer blockage (the verified root cause).
Hold the tyres cured during the stops.
Clean the strainer once.

questions.explain: Correction restores, containment limits impact, and corrective action removes the verified root cause.

questions.text: After a standard is revised because of a verified root cause, what must follow?

options.t: Nothing; the new document is on the server.
Email it to the plant head only.
Issue it under document control, withdraw old copies, train the affected team and verify it is followed.
Wait for the annual audit to check it.

questions.explain: A revised standard changes practice only when it is controlled, trained on and verified.

questions.text: A countermeasure worked on one steam-heated press. Another line has electrically heated presses with no steam strainer. What should happen?

options.t: Don't deploy it there; the failure mechanism doesn't exist. Deploy to presses with the same mechanism, and assess similar-but-different equipment first.
Copy the countermeasure to every press in the plant.
Never share countermeasures outside the original press.
Deploy everywhere without checking, then fix problems later.

questions.explain: Horizontal deployment checks applicability and local conditions before deploying.

questions.text: All actions for a recurring problem show 'Closed' in the tracker. How is effectiveness verified?

options.t: The 'Closed' status proves it.
The action owner confirms verbally.
Compare recurrence data for the original problem measure over a defined period (e.g. stops per shift before vs after) and confirm the actions were implemented.
Ask whether anyone has complained recently.

questions.explain: Marking an action complete does not prove effectiveness; data on the original problem does.
